result.summary: After the Chorus prays for purity and doubts the oracles, Jocasta prays to Apollo. A Corinthian stranger announces that Polybus is dead, and Oedipus feels freed from the prophecy until the stranger reveals he was a foundling taken from a shepherd of Laius. Jocasta, understanding the truth, begs him to stop, then rushes into the Palace, while Oedipus insists on learning his birth.

scenes.title: The Chorus sings of pride and doubt
scenes.summary: The Chorus prays to keep holy laws, warns of tyrannical pride, and fears that faith in oracles and Apollo is failing.
scenes.stakes: Religious faith and the city's piety are shaken by unanswered oracles.

scenes.title: News of Polybus's death
scenes.summary: Jocasta prays to Apollo. A Corinthian stranger arrives and reports that Polybus has died, and Jocasta scorns the oracles.
scenes.stakes: Jocasta fears for her husband's tormented mind.

scenes.title: Oedipus rejoices, still fears
scenes.summary: Oedipus hears the news and doubts the oracle, but still fears marrying his mother Merope and explains Apollo's prophecy.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus fears fulfilling the prophecy of killing his father and marrying his mother.

scenes.title: The foundling revealed
scenes.summary: The stranger reveals Polybus was not Oedipus's father and that he gave Oedipus to the king from Kithairon, from a shepherd of Laius.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus's identity and understanding of his past are overturned.

scenes.title: Jocasta begs and flees
scenes.summary: Jocasta pleads with Oedipus to stop searching, then flees into the Palace. Oedipus resolves to learn his origin, calling himself Fortune's child.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus risks discovering a terrible truth about his birth; Jocasta faces ruin.

alias_notes.explanation: The name Oedipus is explained as meaning 'swollen foot', from the spike through his feet as a baby.
A title of Apollo Lukeios, linked to wolves.

notable_quotes.reason: Explains the meaning of Oedipus's name through his pierced feet.
Oedipus proudly calls himself Fortune's child, deeply ironic before his downfall.

analysis.text: Characters trust chance and doubt prophecy just as truth emerges, creating dramatic irony as Oedipus's relief becomes the path to discovery.
The Chorus's worry about failing oracles reflects Athenian anxieties about religion and the authority of divine prophecy.

legacy.text: Oedipus's name, meaning swollen foot, became part of Freud's 'Oedipus complex' in psychoanalysis.

fun_facts.text: The name Oedipus is often interpreted as 'swollen foot', which the play uses in its plot.

language_notes.text: "The Laws thereof" are the divine, unwritten laws of the gods; "walkers upon ways above" pictures them moving through heaven, not on earth.
"Uncreate" means never created. Olympus, home of the gods, is the father of these laws, and no human made them.
"The leap to that which needs must be" means the fall to inevitable ruin after a climb to the cliff edge.
"Slays askance" means kills from the side, unseen and indirect, like a hidden arrow of fate.
"Dance my dance" refers to the Chorus's sacred dance in worship. They ask why they should perform it if piety goes unrewarded.
Earth's "Heart of Stone" is Delphi, the navel of the world. The Abantes' floor is the temple at Abae in Phocis, and Olympia held the shrine of Zeus.
The wise man judges the future by the past; the line is compressed, and the next sentence says Oedipus fails to do this.
"I steal" means she slips away quietly to the altar; "of right" means Apollo rightfully holds Thebes as his own.
"Not all unclean" asks for some way out of the city's pollution, the plague-bringing guilt of Laius's unavenged murder.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe"; "haply" means perhaps.
The Stranger swears on his own life: let me die in his place if I lie.
"Hie thee" means hurry.
"Call'st thou" is archaic for "do you call"; "thou" is the familiar singular "you" used between husband and wife.
"Give ear" means listen; Jocasta asks him to judge how the priests' oracles come to nothing.
"Pytho's dome" is Apollo's temple at Delphi (Pytho was its old name), where the oracle spoke.
"Birds that shriek" refers to augury, reading omens in the cries and flight of birds.
"Seercraft" means the art of prophecy.
"Warped" means twisted or misled; Oedipus says fear distorted his judgment.
"Hath but Chance above him" means a person ruled only by chance, with no providence overhead; "governance" means control or foresight.
Jocasta says prophets regard a deed done only in a dream as already done; she means the prophecy is harmless, since many men dream of such things.
The tomb refers to Polybus, whose death by natural causes, reported by the Stranger, seems to disprove the prophecy that Oedipus would kill his father.
Elliptical: Oedipus means the stranger must hear the story, and that it concerns Corinth.
"Know my mother's flesh" is a biblical-style euphemism for sexual union; "spill my father's blood" means to murder him.
Archaic 'Tis and 'hath' mark the translation's verse style; the stranger asks whether fear has kept Oedipus away from home in exile.
'Twere well means 'it would be good'; the stranger offers to free Oedipus from his fear.
Defilement means ritual pollution; Oedipus fears incurring it by killing his father and marrying his mother, as the oracle foretold.
'By gift' means Oedipus became Polybus's child through adoption, not birth.
Glen means a narrow mountain valley; Kithairon is the mountain near Thebes where infants were exposed.
Oedipus' own feet could testify: his scarred, damaged ankles are the evidence of what happened to him as an infant.
'Twas is 'it was'; the spike pierced the baby's ankles, which were bound together, though the text says 'feet'.
'Scorn' means cruel treatment; Oedipus bitterly calls the piercing a strange welcome for a newborn.
'Fain' means gladly or willingly; here it suggests people were naturally led to name him after his injury.
The name Oedipus is popularly linked to Greek words meaning 'swollen foot', which the translator renders as 'Who-walks-in-pain'.
'Pale' means an enclosed area or boundary; 'within my pale' means within my realm or hearing.
'Our mistress' means Jocasta, the queen; the Leader suggests she can identify the shepherd.
"The herd" means the herdsman, the shepherd summoned as a witness. "We" is the royal plural Oedipus uses of himself.
Jocasta begs him to forget what he has heard and stop asking; "pray Not to remember" means "I beg you to put it out of mind."
Oedipus means: even if he were a slave's son for three generations back, her own rank would not be tarnished. "Grand-dam" is grandmother.
"Child of woe" is a grieving address to Oedipus; she prays he may never learn the truth.
"Abideth" means remains or stays; "roots" means his origins, and "how low soe'er they be" means however humble.
"Brethren of the sky, the changing Moons" refers to the months, whose waxing and waning match his rise and fall in fortune.

context_notes.text: Jocasta is Oedipus's wife and Creon's sister. Oedipus has just quarrelled with Creon and Tiresias, so the Chorus is left alone to reflect.
Zeus is the king of the gods and the guardian of justice and oaths. The Chorus addresses him here as the supreme god.
Apollo's oracles have been questioned because Jocasta doubted prophecy. The Chorus fears the god is no longer honoured.
Apollo Lukeios, "Slayer of the Wolf" or god of light, was worshipped at Thebes; his oracle had given Oedipus his prophecy.
Corinth was the city where Oedipus was raised as prince, believing Polybus and Merope were his parents.
An oracle had told Oedipus he would kill his father, so he fled Corinth to avoid harming Polybus.
Corinth is the city where Oedipus grew up; he believes Polybus, its king, is his father.
The oracle told Oedipus he would kill his father and marry his mother, which is why he fled Corinth.
Merope is queen of Corinth and wife of Polybus, the couple who raised Oedipus and whom he believes are his true parents.
Apollo's oracle at Delphi gave Oedipus this prophecy, which is why he left Corinth and never returned.
Oedipus fled Corinth because an oracle said he would kill his father and marry his mother; he believes Polybus and Merope are his parents.
Polybus is king of Corinth, who raised Oedipus as his son. The stranger is a Corinthian messenger who has come to announce Polybus's death.
The stranger is a Corinthian herdsman who gave the infant Oedipus to Polybus, king of Corinth, who raised him as his son.
Laius was Jocasta's first husband and king of Thebes, killed before Oedipus arrived. His servant is the key to Oedipus' origin.
The herdsman is the surviving witness to the death of Laius and, as later revealed, to Oedipus's infancy.
Oedipus wrongly supposes Jocasta fears he is low-born, when she has in fact guessed the horrifying truth.

literary_notes.text: Pride is a woman who is drunk and reeling, climbing a mountain and tumbling off the edge, an image of hubris leading to downfall.
The Chorus appeals directly to God to be its guide through confusion, a sudden turn from judging others to prayer.
The question expresses the Chorus's crisis of faith: if the wicked go unpunished, worship seems pointless.
The things of God fading "as mist on the wind" compares the decline of belief to something insubstantial that disperses.
Oedipus is the ship's captain and Thebes the ship; his fear endangers everyone aboard.
Death is given power greater than a king's, turning the Stranger's reply into a grim, neat retort.
Jocasta celebrates Polybus's natural death as disproving oracles, while the audience senses the prophecy may still be fulfilled.
Death is softened into "peace," and the stranger treats an old man's death as a trivial matter.
Oedipus rejoices that he has not killed his father, but the audience senses the truth is not yet uncovered.
The prophecy is imagined as something buried in the grave alongside Polybus, as if it died with him.
Polybus's death is compared to light breaking through darkness, expressing relief and hope.
The audience senses that Merope is not his true mother and that Oedipus's flight from Corinth is bringing the prophecy about.
Praising a mother's face is bitterly ironic, given the prophecy of incest he has just described.
The audience senses the truth is worse than Oedipus hopes; his relief from this fear leads toward the discovery of his real parentage.
Rapid alternating lines of dialogue heighten tension as each answer unsettles Oedipus's understanding of who he is.
Jocasta's dread, unnoticed by the others, shows the audience she already grasps what Oedipus has not yet realised.
Oedipus' half-awakened memory of old pain hints that the truth about his past is about to surface.
His name, taken from his wound, makes his suffering a lasting mark of identity, linking his fate to his body.
Oedipus mocks the Queen's pride while the audience knows her silence comes from dread of the truth about his birth.
Her farewell, "never never more," signals that she will not appear again and that disaster is near.
The Leader likens her silence to a gathering storm about to break, anticipating coming catastrophe.
Fortune is made a smiling mother and the Moons her siblings, casting Oedipus's life as ruled by chance; the irony is that fate, not luck, rules him.
